shortlist.raw_text: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

shortlist.raw_text: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

shortlist.raw_text: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now. This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life. I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new. That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era. There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go. shortlist.summary: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. shortlist.raw_text: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.

shortlist.title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
shortlist.summary: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. shortlist.raw_text: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

Coverage from The Hacker News: "Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes Passwords and Keys in 1,122 Public Copies on GitHub"
Claude Code saves secrets in approved commands, exposing 2,539 credentials across 1,994 public GitHub repositories, Apiiro finds.

Coverage from iTWire: "Claude Code approval files found exposing company secrets on GitHub, says Apirro researchers"
David M Williams | Published 7 Nov 2026
Apiiro researchers say remembered commands are carrying credentials into public repositories, exposing a gap between approving an agent’s work and controlling what it leaves behind.
You ask your AI coding assistant to check a database connection. It proposes a command, asks permission, and offers to stop interrupting you for that command in future. You approve it and get on with your work.
What you may not realise is that the approval itself can become another copy of your database password.
That is the problem examined in research published on 5 November by Apiiro’s Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi . They say Claude Code can retain a complete approved shell command, including credentials, in .claude/settings.local.json. If that file is committed and pushed to a public repository, the credentials go with it.
The researchers examined 104,185 public copies of that local settings file and classified 1,122, or about 1.1%, as containing secrets. Those files held 1,379 distinct values. Their broader investigation, including Git history, shared settings and agent transcripts, counted 2,539 distinct secrets across 1,994 repositories.
It's important to note Apiiro did not try the credentials. Its classification identifies likely credentials from their format and context, and the research does not prove every one (or any one) still works. The findings establish an exposure risk - rather than an actual demonstrated breach.
Claude Code’s own documentation confirms that choosing “Yes, and don’t ask again” for a Bash command saves an allow rule in the project’s local settings file. This lets the tool run matching commands without repeatedly seeking approval.
The file is intended for personal settings, rather than something shared with everyone working on the project. Anthropic says the first time Claude Code writes it inside a Git repository, it adds an entry to the developer’s global Git excludes file if needed. That is a real protection, and it must be noted Claude is not simply publishing secrets by default.
However, a global exclusion belongs to that developer’s machine. It does not travel with the project in the way a committed .gitignore file does. There is also a separate problem if the settings file has already been tracked: Git’s documentation explicitly says ignore rules do not affect files already under version control.
This distinction is pretty easy to miss. A filename containing “local” describes how the application us

Coverage from note: "[ClaudeCode Incident] 7 Security Incidents Actually Caused by 'Minor Operational or Configuration Errors' and Countermeasures You Can Take Starting Today"
Claude Code deleted the entire contents of the home folder.
In October 2025, this report was posted on GitHub. What appeared in the terminal were thousands of lines of messages saying 'Permission denied' when it tried to delete /bin and /etc. While system files protected by permissions remained, almost all of the user's personal files were gone.
The AI did not destroy them on purpose. Most accidents start with 'minor operations' and 'minor configuration errors' on the human side. Giving permission without reading the confirmation carefully. Thinking a setting was active when it actually wasn't.
I have been working as an app engineer for 5 years, and I currently operate an app I built with Claude Code by myself. Since it is a tool I use every day, this is not someone else's problem. Therefore, I researched and summarized actual accidents that occurred and cases published by security companies.
All cases are those I have verified by opening the original reports or articles from security companies. The sources are listed together at the end.
This is the case mentioned at the beginning. In the GitHub report (October 2025, Claude Code 2.0.22, Linux environment inside Windows), a command was executed to delete from the root (/) when it should have been working in the project folder.
Around the same time, a similar story was posted on Reddit regarding a Mac. When it was asked to organize an old repository, the command left in the record was as follows.
The ~/ at the end means 'my home folder'. It is reported that because of this one character, everything from desktop files to password information was deleted.
It is unclear whether this person was using a 'skip all confirmations mode' or if a confirmation appeared but they gave permission without reading it carefully. However, in either case, the human allowed a deletion command to pass without reading it is common.
If rm (delete), git push (send), or git reset --hard (delete work) appear, always read one line before giving permission
Do not select 'don't ask again' for deletion-type commands
Writing files you don't want Claude Code to read (like .env) in a file called .claudeignore. This is a method often seen on the internet, but in a verification by The Register in January 2026, it read the .env written in .claudeignore as requested (Claude Code 2.1.12).
Moreover, an example is introduced where Claude itself gave the user the incorrect explanation that 'if you write it in .claudeignore, it won't read it'.
What 

Background (Configuration file, Wikipedia):
A configuration file, also known as config file, is a file that stores data used to configure a software system such as an application, a server or an operating system.

Background (White-box cryptography, Wikipedia):
In cryptography, the white-box model refers to an extreme attack scenario, in which an adversary has full unrestricted access to a cryptographic implementation, most commonly of a block cipher such as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). A variety of security goals may be posed, the most fundamental being "unbreakability", requiring that any (bounded) attacker should not be able to extract the secret key hardcoded in the implementation, while at the same time the implementation must be fully functional. In contrast, the black-box model only provides oracle access to the analyzed cryptographic primitive. There is also a model in-between, the so-called gray-box model, which corresponds to additional information leakage from the implementation, more commonly referred to as side-channel leakage.

text:
Over 2,500 database keys and passwords recently surfaced in public GitHub repositories.

The exposure did not require a corporate network breach. 

Anthropic's Claude Code CLI asks developers for permission before running shell commands. Selecting "Yes, and don't ask again" silences future prompts, but it also writes the complete approved command, raw credentials included, into a local settings file.

Security firm Apiiro scanned GitHub for these settings files and reported the following:
• 104,185 public copies examined
• 1,122 files contained exposed secrets
• 2,539 total distinct credentials exposed across 1,994 public repositories

Anthropic attempts to prevent commits by setting a global Git exclude rule on the developer's machine. However, global rules stay on that specific computer and do not travel with the project repository. Furthermore, Git ignore rules do not apply to files already under version control.

Apiiro notes it did not attempt to log in with the credentials, so some keys may no longer be active. 

The incident highlights a practical gap between granting an AI agent permission and controlling the local configuration files it leaves behind.

Source: apiiro.com, with reporting from The Hacker News and iTWire

alt_openings:
Option 1 (Tool as subject):
Anthropic's Claude Code tool exposed 2,539 passwords in public GitHub repositories.
It happened because developers clicked a prompt meant to save them time.
When to prefer: Best for engineering audiences who immediately recognize Claude Code and care about developer tooling issues.

Option 2 (Your X):
Your developers might be pushing database passwords to GitHub without knowing it.
A setting designed to reduce popups in AI tools is silently saving credentials to tracked files.
When to prefer: Best for founders, CTOs, and managers who oversee technical teams and care about immediate organizational risk.

Option 3 (Story in motion):
A developer clicked "don't ask again" on an AI shell prompt.
Minutes later, the raw database key inside that command was visible to anyone on GitHub.
When to prefer: Best for a general management audience, using narrative structure to explain a technical human-error problem.

Pick: Option 2 (Your X). It creates immediate accountability for managers and founders, forcing them to click "see more" to confirm whether their own team's workflow is exposed.
